newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordanian soldier's lawyers say Israel still enemy.
newsitem.headline: Jordanian soldier's lawyers say Israel still enemy.

text.p: Lawyers for a Jordanian soldier who shot dead seven Israeli girls in March challenged testimony from their schoolfriends on Sunday, saying Israelis were Jordan's enemy and their words worthless.

They said that despite a 1994 peace treaty between Jordan and Israel, military judges at the trial of Private Ahmed Daqamsa should reject the Israeli statements because they came from Jews who declined to speak under oath.

"The defence insists on the illegality of hearing Jewish witnesses and (hearing) each one who refuses to give an oath," chief defence lawyer Hussein Majalli told the court at the start of Sunday's session.
Brigadier Mamoun al-Khasawneh rejected Majalli's challenge, but it was echoed by other members of Daqamsa's defence team and by Jordanian opponents of close ties with Israel.
"Their testimony is invalid. They are still the enemy," Samih Khreis, another member of Daqamsa's defence, told reporters during a recess.
Daqamsa's family, barred from the court while Israelis gave evidence, picnicked by the roadside and declared him a hero.

"I hold my head up high because I am the wife of Ahmed Daqamsa," his wife Fatima told reporters outside the military base. She said authorities tried to prevent members of Daqamsa's tribe from even travelling to Amman for Sunday's hearing.
"Ahmed Daqamsa is not alone," she said.

Inside the court three schoolgirls and a teacher from their religious school near Jerusalem recalled the scene when Daqamsa opened fire at them in Jordan's border territory of Baqoura, leased to Israel under the peace accord.
The witnesses, brought to the heavily guarded military base a few miles (km) south of Amman, included 14-year-old twins Hela and Keren Ivri, both lightly wounded in the shooting.
Hela glanced back nervously at Daqamsa as he sat impassively behind a black metal cage in the dock.

"This is the island where peace was made with Jordan," Hela quoted their guide as saying as the group arrived in Baqoura, where Jordan's King Hussein met former Israeli Prime Minister Yitzak Rabin in 1995 to discuss joint water plans.
Jordanian soldiers patrol the small patch of land, rising above the confluence of the Jordan and Yarmouk rivers. Israelis have virtually free access and Israeli farmers own land there.
Israelis call it "the Island of Peace" but Jordanian opponents of the peace deal say their land was surrendered.
"Baqoura is a Trojan Horse. It is the first Israeli settlement in Jordan," said Laith Shubailat, head of Jordan's Islamist-dominated Engineers Union who has attended most sessions of Daqamsa's trial.
Salem Nahhas, leader of the opposition Hashd Party, said this week that sympathy for Daqamsa was prompted by a sense of betrayal over Baqoura.

"For the first time Jordanian people know that there is an occupied land called Baqoura," he said. "The government said we had regained all our land (under the peace treaty) but this clash in Baqoura has shown it is not true."
King Hussein said Daqamsa's action had shamed the army and he should have been shot dead on the spot. Last week he received Israeli witnesses who had testified at the court.
Daqamsa has not denied shooting the girls, six of them 13 years old and one 11, but says he acted impulsively after being provoked during Moslem prayers.
He is charged with premeditated murder and faces a death sentence if found guilty.
